issues.legal_issue: An ostensibly absolute conveyance with a condition of reconveyance is a mortgage by conditional sale when the deed and surrounding circumstances show that the transfer secures a debt and creates a debtor-creditor relationship.
material_facts: The transferors were indebted and used the consideration to discharge debts owed to a bank and to the transferees and their associates.

The deed provided for reconveyance at the stated prices and also allowed the transferees, after a specified period, to require the transferors to take back properties and repay the consideration, including where the properties had been adversely affected by circumstances beyond the transferees’ control.
A same-day agreement required the transferors to pay the difference between net rents and interest on the consideration until reconveyance.
The properties were worth substantially more than the prices stated in the deed.
The transferors brought a suit for redemption, contending that the conveyance was a mortgage.
issues.conclusion: The transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale, not an absolute sale with a right of repurchase, and the transferors could redeem the properties. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, including its proviso added by Act XX of 1929, a mortgage by conditional sale requires the condition to be embodied in the instrument effecting or purporting to effect the sale. Incorporation of the condition does not by itself establish a mortgage: the parties’ intention must be determined from the deed read with surrounding circumstances. The distinction is whether the transfer creates a debtor-creditor relationship and provides security for a debt, or instead creates an outright sale subject to an obligation to retransfer. The form of the deed, and a strict time limit for repurchase, are not decisive. The Court relied on Narasingerji Gyanagerji v. Panuganti Parthasarathi and Others (1924) L.R. 51 I.A. 305.

rule.if: redemption_action and (transferors_were_indebted or repayment_interest_covenant) and transferees_could_require_takeback and consideration_was_inadequate

predicates.redemption_action: The transferors brought a proceeding seeking redemption of the transferred property.
predicates.transferors_were_indebted: The transferors owed debts when they made the transfer, and the consideration was used to discharge those debts.
predicates.repayment_interest_covenant: The transferors agreed to make payments calculated by reference to interest on the consideration until reconveyance.
predicates.transferees_could_require_takeback: The transferees could require the transferors to take back the property and repay the consideration.
predicates.consideration_was_inadequate: The consideration stated for the property was substantially below its value.
predicates.transaction_is_a_redeemable_mortgage: The transaction is treated as a mortgage that the transferors may redeem.

issues.definition: When a redemption action concerns an indebted transfer with the stated repayment and takeback features and inadequate consideration, the transaction is treated as a redeemable mortgage.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s subsequent conduct is inadmissible as evidence of the character of a transaction when construing the instrument that created it.
material_facts: The transferees sought to rely on the transferors’ conduct after the transaction to support their characterization of it as a sale.
The Court considered the transaction by construing the deed in light of surrounding circumstances and contemporaneous conduct.
issues.conclusion: The evidence of subsequent conduct was inadmissible for determining the character of the transaction.
issues.legal_principle: In construing a deed, oral evidence of intention cannot be used to interpret its covenants. Evidence may explain or contradict recitals, as distinct from the document’s terms, and contemporaneous conduct is admissible as a surrounding circumstance. Subsequent conduct is inadmissible. The Court relied on Narasingerji Gyanagerji v. Panuganti Parthasarathi and Others (1924) L.R. 51 I.A. 305.

predicates.instrument_character_dispute: The proceeding requires a court to determine the character of a transaction from its instrument.
predicates.party_relies_on_post_execution_conduct: A party offers conduct occurring after the instrument was made as evidence of the transaction’s character.
predicates.post_execution_conduct_is_inadmissible_t: Post-execution conduct cannot be used to determine the character of the transaction.

issues.definition: When a party relies on later conduct in a dispute about an instrument’s character, that conduct cannot determine the instrument’s character.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered agreement is admissible to evidence a personal covenant that does not create, declare, limit, or extinguish an interest in immovable property, but not to establish an alteration of the instrument’s terms concerning reconveyance.
material_facts: The parties executed a separate agreement on the same day as the conveyance.
The agreement required the transferors to pay the difference between net rent and interest on the consideration until reconveyance.
The transferees argued that the agreement was inadmissible because it was not registered.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was admissible insofar as it evidenced the personal covenant to pay interest, but it could not be used without registration to establish an alteration of the reconveyance terms in the registered instrument.
issues.legal_principle: A document that does not purport to create, declare, limit, or extinguish an interest in immovable property need not be excluded for want of registration when it is offered to evidence a personal covenant. A separate agreement containing a condition relating to reconveyance cannot, without registration, be admitted to evidence an alteration of the registered instrument’s reconveyance terms.

predicates.instrument_interpretation_dispute: The proceeding requires the court to determine the effect of an instrument concerning immovable property.
predicates.unregistered_agreement_contains_personal: A separate unregistered agreement records a personal promise to make payments and does not itself create or alter an interest in the property.
predicates.unregistered_agreement_is_admissible_to_: The unregistered agreement may be admitted to prove the personal payment promise, but not to alter the instrument’s reconveyance terms.

issues.definition: When an unregistered agreement records a personal payment promise in a dispute about an instrument concerning immovable property, it may prove that promise but not alter the instrument’s reconveyance terms.
